en.title: Crop Science: the whole course
en.short: What crop science is, how the degree is organised, the main areas, how to study, and common mistakes.

sections.heading: What crop science is
sections.text: Crop science is the study of plants grown for food, feed, fibre, fuel and other products, and of the systems used to produce them. It draws on plant biology, soil science, ecology, genetics, economics and engineering. Agronomy is the management of field crops. Horticulture is the production of fruits, vegetables and ornamental plants. Plant breeding is the genetic improvement of crops. Crop protection covers weeds, animal pests such as insects, mites, nematodes and rodents, and diseases. The subject matters because crop production supplies food and raw materials, supports incomes and trade, and affects land, water and biodiversity. It is both a science and a practice.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text: Programmes differ by country and institution. In Nigeria, universities award BSc or BAgric in agriculture, crop science or related fields; polytechnics award the National Diploma (ND) and Higher National Diploma (HND) in agricultural technology or crop production; and colleges of education award the Nigeria Certificate in Education (NCE). A university programme commonly takes four or five years depending on the institution and entry route, and may include practical training. In England, a BSc usually takes three years, with an optional placement year. In Ghana and Kenya, BSc agriculture programmes commonly take four years. A master’s degree usually takes one to two years and ends with a dissertation. These are general patterns only. Always check your own handbook for the award, length, entry requirements and regulations.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The introductory stage starts with the scope and history of crop science and the global importance of crops. It then moves through seed structure and germination; root, stem and leaf morphology; flowers, pollination, seeds and fruits; photosynthesis, respiration and growth; development, hormones and photoperiodism; mineral nutrition and water relations; soil properties and fertility; crop classification, adaptation and agro-ecology; and weather, climate and the cropping calendar.

The core stage covers production practice: land preparation and tillage; planting methods, plant population and spacing; weed, pest and disease management; fertiliser use; irrigation and water management; cropping systems, rotation and intercropping; growth analysis and yield components; harvesting, threshing and postharvest handling; seed production and certification; plant breeding; biotechnology and genetically modified crops; climate change and resilience; pasture and forage crops; industrial and plantation crops; production economics and farm management; farm power and mechanisation; pesticide safety, regulation and environmental care; research methods and field trial design; analysis of experimental data and reporting; and professional ethics.

At master’s level, advanced crop physiology and source-sink relations, quantitative genetics and genomics, cropping systems modelling and decision support, and dissertation research methods deepen the same themes.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text: Learn each topic at three levels: the plant or field process, the management decision, and the measurement. For example, when studying fertiliser use, know how roots take up nitrogen, how a recommendation is calculated from a soil test, and how a field trial measures response. Draw diagrams of plant parts and label them from memory. Keep a glossary of terms such as source (where sugar is made), sink (where it is used or stored), photoperiod (day length) and economic threshold (the pest level at which control should start, before damage exceeds the cost of control). Visit a farm or trial plot if you can, and compare what you see with the textbook. Practise calculations for seed rate, plant population, fertiliser dose and yield. Read the label of any pesticide you study and note the safety rules. For research methods, learn why randomisation, replication and control plots matter. Use a spreadsheet or statistical package for simple analysis. Record the date, place and method behind any figure you quote.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Students memorise definitions without linking them to a crop or field problem. They confuse plant population with spacing, or yield per plant with yield per hectare. They treat a pesticide as harmless because it is legal, or ignore the pre-harvest interval, the waiting period before harvest. They compare yields or prices from different years or countries without checking the method. In breeding, they confuse phenotype (what a plant looks like) with genotype (its genetic make-up). In experiments, they change more than one factor at a time or fail to keep a control. In essays, they present one country’s regulation as universal. Always name the crop, the country and the year when a rule or figure depends on them.

keyPoints: Crop science applies plant biology, soil science, ecology, genetics, economics and engineering to crop production.
Degree length and awards vary by country and institution, so check your handbook.
Study each topic as a plant process, a management decision and a measurement.
Weeds, pests and diseases are managed by combining several methods, not by one chemical alone.
Field trials need replication, randomisation and a control.
Name the crop, country and year when a rule or figure depends on them.

en.title: Crop Science: Scope, Origins and Global Importance
en.short: Definitions, centres of origin, spread and importance of crops in food, feed and industry.

sections.heading: What crop science is
sections.text:
Crop science is the scientific study of crop plants: how they grow, how they are improved, protected, produced and used. A crop is a plant grown on purpose for food, feed, fibre, fuel or other products. Agronomy is the branch of agricultural science that deals with field crop production and the management of the soil and environment in which crops grow.

Crop science sits among related disciplines. Plant science explains growth, genetics and pests; soil science explains nutrient and water supply; agricultural economics explains costs, prices and farm decisions. Crop science integrates these to answer practical questions: which crop, field, inputs and return.

sections.heading: Centres of origin
sections.text: Nikolai Vavilov, a Russian plant scientist, proposed centres of origin, regions where crops were first domesticated. Modern evidence shows many crops arose in more than one region. Wheat, barley, lentil and chickpea come from the Fertile Crescent, an arc of fertile land in the Middle East from the Persian Gulf to the eastern Mediterranean. Rice comes from Asia, with African rice domesticated separately in West Africa. Maize comes from Mesoamerica (Mexico and Central America); sorghum and pearl millet from Africa; soybean from China; common bean and potato from the Americas; cassava and groundnut from South America; white yam from West Africa.

sections.heading: Spread of crops
sections.text: After 1492 the Columbian exchange carried maize, cassava, potato, sweet potato and groundnut from the Americas to Africa, Asia and Europe. Wheat and rice moved earlier along trade and migration routes. In West Africa, maize and cassava became staple foods; in Nigeria, cassava is now a major food and industrial crop. Farmers also moved crops between ecological zones, selecting types that suited local rainfall and soils.

sections.heading: Why crops matter
sections.text: Crops feed people as sources of energy and protein. Cereals supply most human calories; legumes add protein; root crops give energy and often grow where rainfall is uncertain. Crops also feed animals, especially maize, sorghum and forage. Industry uses crops for oil, sugar, starch, fibre and beverages. Amina in Kano grows sorghum and cowpea for food and cash; her cousin in Ogun grows cassava for garri and starch. Crop science helps farmers raise yield and reduce loss.

keyPoints: Crop science studies crop plants and their production, improvement, protection and use.
Agronomy is the field-crop production branch of agricultural science, linking plant science, soil science and agricultural economics.
Vavilov’s centres of origin are broad regions of domestication, and modern evidence shows many crops arose in more than one region.
Major cereals, legumes and root crops came from the Fertile Crescent, Asia, Africa and the Americas, then spread through trade, migration and the Columbian exchange.
Crops supply human calories and protein, livestock feed, and industrial raw materials such as oil, sugar, starch and fibre.
Crop science helps farmers choose crops and manage them to raise yield and reduce loss.

en.title: Seed Structure, Germination and Seedling Establishment
en.short: Seed parts in monocots and dicots, germination conditions, dormancy, vigour and planting depth.

sections.heading: Parts of the seed
sections.text: A dicot seed such as cowpea has a seed coat (testa), two cotyledons that store food, and an embryo with a radicle (future root) and a plumule (future shoot). A monocot seed such as maize has one cotyledon, called the scutellum, a starchy endosperm, and an embryo. In cereals the seed coat is fused with the fruit wall, and the whole grain is called a caryopsis. The aleurone layer, just under the coat, helps break down endosperm food at germination.

sections.heading: Conditions and stages
sections.text: Germination needs water, oxygen and a suitable temperature. Water is taken up first in imbibition, a physical process driven by the dry seed tissues. Enzymes then become active and break stored starch and protein into simpler substances for the embryo. The radicle emerges first, then the plumule. In epigeal germination the cotyledons are lifted above the soil; in hypogeal germination they stay below. Oxygen is needed for respiration, so waterlogging or a hard soil crust can smother the seed.

sections.heading: Dormancy, vigour, depth
sections.text: Dormancy is the failure of a viable seed to germinate even when conditions are favourable. Causes include a hard, impermeable seed coat, an immature embryo, or inhibitors such as abscisic acid. Seed vigour is the ability to germinate quickly and produce normal seedlings, including under stress. Planting depth matters: too shallow and the seed dries out; too deep and the seedling uses up its stored food before reaching light. Large seeds can emerge from deeper sowing than small ones. For example, maize sown about 4 to 5 cm deep in moist soil usually emerges within a week, but the time varies with temperature and variety.

keyPoints: A dicot seed has two cotyledons; a monocot seed has one, the scutellum.
Germination requires water, oxygen and a suitable temperature.
Imbibition is the first stage, followed by enzyme activity and radicle emergence.
Dormancy is a block to germination in a viable seed, not a lack of viability.
High-vigour seed germinates quickly and produces normal seedlings, even under stress.
Sow at the recommended depth: too shallow dries out, too deep exhausts reserves.

en.title: Crop Plant Structure: Roots, Stems and Leaves
en.short: Root and shoot systems, tillering, leaf types, and how form supports uptake, photosynthesis and lodging resistance.

sections.heading: Root systems
sections.text: Roots are the below-ground vegetative organs. A taproot system has one main root with side roots, common in many dicotyledons (dicots) such as cowpea. A fibrous system has many similar roots, common in monocotyledons (monocots) such as maize and rice. Root hairs are tiny extensions of epidermal cells; they increase the surface for water and nutrient uptake. Roots also anchor the plant and may store food. Most absorption occurs near root tips, where young hairs are active.

sections.heading: Stems and tillering
sections.text: The stem bears leaves and flowers. It has nodes, where leaves and buds arise, and internodes between them. Vascular bundles carry water and minerals upward in xylem and sugars in phloem. Cereal stems have scattered vascular bundles and no cambium, so they do not thicken like dicot stems. In cereals such as rice, wheat and maize, side shoots called tillers grow from basal nodes near the soil. In many dicots, side branches grow from axillary buds. Stem strength and root anchorage together resist lodging, the permanent falling over of a crop.

sections.heading: Leaves
sections.text: A leaf is a flat blade, the lamina, joined to the stem by a petiole. Grasses have a sheath around the stem and a blade with parallel veins; many dicots have net veins and a petiole. Leaves may be simple or compound and are arranged alternately, oppositely or in whorls. The blade holds mesophyll cells where photosynthesis occurs. Stomata allow gas exchange, and veins supply water and remove sugars.

sections.heading: Form and lodging
sections.text: A deep root system holds the plant and reaches water. Strong, short stems and upright leaves support the canopy and reduce shading. Lodging resistance depends on stem thickness and strength, root anchorage and disease-free tissues. Imagine a rice field near Abakaliki, Nigeria: a tall variety with long weak stems falls after wind and rain, while a shorter stiff-stemmed variety stands. The fallen crop is harder to harvest and grain may rot.

keyPoints: Roots absorb water and nutrients mainly through young root hairs and anchor the plant.
Taproot systems are common in dicots and fibrous systems in monocots such as cereals.
Stems have nodes and internodes and transport water, minerals and sugars.
Tillers are basal side shoots in cereals, while many dicots branch from axillary buds.
Leaves are the main photosynthetic organs, and grass leaves have sheaths and parallel veins.
Lodging resistance depends on stem strength, root anchorage and healthy tissues.

en.title: Flowers, Pollination, Seeds and Fruits in Crops
en.short: Flower structure, pollination, fertilisation, seed and fruit formation, and crop breeding systems.

sections.heading: Flower structure
sections.text:
A flower is a shoot modified for reproduction. The outer whorls are the sepals, which protect the bud, and the petals, which attract pollinators. Inside are the stamens, each with an anther that makes pollen, held on a filament; and one or more carpels, each with a stigma that receives pollen, a style, and an ovary containing ovules.

Monocots usually have flower parts in threes, pollen with one furrow, and one cotyledon. Dicots usually have flower parts in fours or fives, pollen with three furrows, and two cotyledons. These are general patterns, and exceptions occur.

sections.heading: Pollination and fertilisation
sections.text:
Pollination is the transfer of pollen to a stigma. Self-pollination moves pollen within one flower or plant; cross-pollination moves it between plants. Agents include wind (maize), insects (many fruits and vegetables), water, birds and bats.

Fertilisation follows. The pollen grain germinates and a tube grows down the style to the ovule. In angiosperms two male nuclei enter: one fuses with the egg to form the zygote, the other with two polar nuclei to form endosperm, the food store. This is double fertilisation. The ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit.

sections.heading: Breeding systems
sections.text:
Crops are grouped by how they breed. Self-pollinated crops include rice, wheat, tomato and cowpea; their flowers often pollinate before opening. Cross-pollinated crops include maize, oil palm and cassava. Vegetatively propagated crops are multiplied from stems, roots or tubers, for example yam, cassava, sweet potato and banana.

The groups overlap: cassava is cross-pollinated yet propagated by stem cuttings.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text:
Self-pollinated crops are easy to fix as pure lines, but crossing them needs hand emasculation, removing the anthers before they shed pollen. Cross-pollinated crops show inbreeding depression and need isolation to keep purity; hybrid maize is made by detasselling the female rows, cutting off their male tassels. Vegetative crops keep a genotype intact but pass on viruses.

Case: Ngozi’s seed field of 2,000 plants has 40 off-types. 40 ÷ 2,000 × 100 = 2%. She rogues them out, that is, removes them. Isolation distances are set by national seed regulations, so check the current rule.

keyPoints: A stamen has an anther and filament; a carpel has stigma, style and ovary.
Monocot flowers usually have parts in threes; dicot flowers in fours or fives.
Double fertilisation forms both the zygote and the endosperm.
The ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit.
Self-pollinated crops are bred as pure lines; cross-pollinated crops need isolation.
Vegetatively propagated crops keep a genotype intact but can carry viruses.

en.title: Photosynthesis, Respiration and Crop Growth
en.short: Light and dark reactions, photorespiration, C3 C4 CAM crops, respiration, LAI and crop growth rate.

sections.heading: Light and dark reactions
sections.text: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy. In the light reactions, chlorophyll in the thylakoid membranes splits water, releases oxygen, and makes ATP and NADPH. In the dark reactions, also called the Calvin cycle, the enzyme RuBisCO fixes carbon dioxide in the stroma. ATP and NADPH then reduce the fixed carbon to triose phosphate, which becomes sucrose or starch. The dark reactions do not need light directly, but they depend on the light reactions.

sections.heading: Photorespiration and pathways
sections.text: RuBisCO can bind oxygen instead of carbon dioxide, especially when stomata close in warm, dry conditions. This is photorespiration; it wastes carbon and energy. C3 plants form a three-carbon first product and include rice, wheat and cassava. C4 plants form a four-carbon first product and concentrate carbon dioxide around RuBisCO, so photorespiration is low; examples are maize, sorghum and sugarcane. CAM plants open stomata at night, store carbon dioxide as organic acids, and use it by day; examples are pineapple and Agave.

sections.heading: Respiration and dry matter
sections.text: Respiration in mitochondria breaks down assimilates, using oxygen to release energy for growth and maintenance, and gives off carbon dioxide and water. Net dry matter accumulation is the assimilate produced by photosynthesis minus respiration and other losses. More leaf area usually means more light intercepted, but very high leaf area index shades lower leaves. Leaf area index (LAI) is leaf area ÷ ground area.

sections.heading: Growth analysis example
sections.text: Crop growth rate (CGR) is dry matter increase per unit ground area per unit time: CGR = (W2 − W1) ÷ (t2 − t1). Suppose a 4 m² plot has 200 g dry mass at day 10 and 440 g at day 20. W1 = 200 ÷ 4 = 50 g m−2; W2 = 440 ÷ 4 = 110 g m−2. CGR = (110 − 50) ÷ (20 − 10) = 6 g m−2 d−1. LAI from 8 m² leaf area is 8 ÷ 4 = 2.0.

keyPoints: Light reactions make ATP and NADPH and release oxygen; the Calvin cycle uses them to fix carbon dioxide.
Photorespiration wastes carbon and energy when RuBisCO binds oxygen, especially in C3 plants under heat and drought.
C4 and CAM plants reduce photorespiration by concentrating carbon dioxide; maize and sugarcane are C4, pineapple is CAM.
Respiration uses assimilates, so net dry matter is photosynthesis minus respiration and losses.
LAI = leaf area ÷ ground area; CGR = (W2 − W1) ÷ (t2 − t1), with W as dry mass per ground area.
High LAI can shade lower leaves, so maximum crop growth occurs at an optimum LAI, not the highest possible LAI.

en.title: Plant Development, Growth Regulators and Photoperiodism
en.short: Cell growth, the five growth regulator classes, vernalisation, photoperiodism and flowering phases.

sections.heading: Growth and development
sections.text: Growth is an irreversible increase in size or mass. Development is the ordered change in form and function, including flowering. Growth starts in meristems, where cells divide by mitosis. New cells then elongate, mainly by taking up water and loosening their walls. Finally they differentiate into specialised cells such as xylem vessels or root hairs. Division, elongation and differentiation overlap.

sections.heading: Five regulator classes
sections.text: Plant growth regulators are natural or synthetic substances that influence growth and development. The five main classes are auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid and ethylene. Auxins promote cell elongation, apical dominance and root formation. Gibberellins promote stem elongation, seed germination and fruit growth. Cytokinins promote cell division, shoot formation and delay leaf ageing. Abscisic acid closes stomata under drought and maintains seed dormancy. Ethylene promotes fruit ripening, leaf fall and senescence. Effects depend on concentration, tissue and stage.

sections.heading: Photoperiodism
sections.text: Photoperiodism is the response of plants to the lengths of day and night. Flowering is controlled by the length of the dark period, not the length of the day. Short-day plants flower when the night is longer than a critical night length. Long-day plants flower when the night is shorter than it. Day-neutral plants flower over a wide range of day lengths. For example, a short-day plant with a critical night length of 10 hours flowers under a 12-hour night but not under a 9-hour night. A light break can prevent flowering in short-day plants.

sections.heading: Vernalisation and phases
sections.text: Vernalisation is the promotion of flowering by a period of low temperature, as in winter wheat and many biennials. It is separate from photoperiodism, though both may be needed. A plant passes through a juvenile phase, when it cannot flower, then a vegetative phase of leaf and stem growth, then a reproductive phase when it flowers. The juvenile phase length varies with species and cultivar. Farmers use these responses to choose sowing dates and varieties that match their season.

keyPoints: Growth is an irreversible increase in size or mass, while development includes changes such as flowering.
Cells divide in meristems, elongate by water uptake and wall loosening, then differentiate into specialised tissues.
The five main growth regulator classes are auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid and ethylene.
Short-day plants flower when the night exceeds their critical night length; long-day plants flower when the night is shorter.
Vernalisation is low-temperature promotion of flowering and is separate from photoperiodism.
Flowering depends on passing from the juvenile phase to the vegetative phase and then the reproductive phase.

en.title: Mineral Nutrition and Water Relations of Crops
en.short: Essential minerals, deficiency symptoms, nutrient uptake, transpiration, water potential and soil water limits.

sections.heading: Essential mineral elements
sections.text:
Plants need 17 essential elements. Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen come from air and water; the other 14 are minerals. Nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulphur are needed in large amounts, so they are macronutrients. Iron, manganese, zinc, copper, boron, molybdenum, chlorine and nickel are needed in tiny amounts, so they are micronutrients.

Each element has a job. Nitrogen builds proteins and chlorophyll, so shortage gives pale older leaves. Phosphorus carries energy, so shortage gives stunted plants with purplish leaves. Potassium regulates water and enzymes, and shortage scorches leaf edges. Calcium and boron build cell walls, so shortage damages growing tips. Symptoms vary with crop, soil and variety, so confirm with soil or leaf analysis.

sections.heading: Nutrient uptake by roots
sections.text: Ions reach a root in three ways: root interception (the root grows into them), mass flow (carried in water moving towards the root) and diffusion (movement down a concentration gradient). Uptake across the root membrane uses carrier proteins. Some uptake is passive, but most is active transport, which needs energy from respiration. Mycorrhizal fungi extend the reach of roots, especially for phosphorus.

sections.heading: Water potential and transpiration
sections.text: Water moves from high to low water potential, a measure of the free energy of water. Pure water at atmospheric pressure is zero; solutions are negative. Roots absorb water, it moves up the xylem, and most leaves the plant as transpiration through stomata, driven by the vapour pressure difference between leaf and air. Transpiration cools the leaf and pulls water and nutrients upward, but it costs water.

sections.heading: Field capacity and wilting point
sections.text:
Field capacity is the water left in soil after free drainage. Permanent wilting point is where plants can no longer extract water. The difference is the available water capacity.

Example: field capacity 25% and wilting point 12% by mass, bulk density 1.3 g/cm³, rooting depth 300 mm.
Available water = (0.25 − 0.12) × 1.3 × 300 = 50.7 mm.

In rain-fed farming, rainfall timing and amount decide how much of that is refilled, so drought at flowering often limits yield most.

keyPoints: Plants need 17 essential elements; 14 are minerals taken up by roots.
Macronutrients are needed in large amounts, micronutrients in tiny amounts.
Nutrients reach roots by interception, mass flow and diffusion.
Most ion uptake is active transport and needs respiratory energy.
Water moves from high to low water potential; transpiration is the main loss.
Available water = (field capacity − wilting point) × bulk density × rooting depth.

en.title: Soils for Crop Production: Properties and Fertility
en.short: Soil texture, structure, organic matter, pH, CEC, fertility, fertilisers and soil health.

sections.heading: Texture and structure
sections.text: Soil texture is the proportion of sand, silt and clay particles. Sandy soils drain quickly but hold few nutrients; clay soils hold water and nutrients but can be sticky and poorly aerated. Structure is how particles stick into aggregates. Good structure gives pores for roots, air and water. Compaction and crusting restrict rooting. Organic matter binds aggregates and improves both sandy and clay soils.

sections.heading: pH, CEC and fertility
sections.text: Soil pH measures acidity or alkalinity on a scale from 0 to 14. Most crops grow best near pH 6 to 7, but this varies. At low pH, aluminium can harm roots and phosphorus becomes less available. Cation exchange capacity (CEC) is the soil’s ability to hold exchangeable cations such as calcium, magnesium, potassium and ammonium. It is measured in cmol(+)/kg. High CEC, common in clay and organic soils, reduces leaching. Example: a soil holds 4 cmol(+)/kg calcium and 1 cmol(+)/kg magnesium. Its CEC from these cations is 5 cmol(+)/kg. Fertility is the soil’s capacity to supply nutrients in available forms. It depends on texture, organic matter, pH and CEC, not on one test alone.

sections.heading: Fertilisers and soil health
sections.text: Fertilisers supply nutrients. Inorganic fertilisers include straight fertilisers with one main nutrient, such as urea for nitrogen, and compound fertilisers with two or more. Organic fertilisers such as manure and compost supply nutrients slowly and add organic matter. Apply fertiliser according to soil tests and crop needs; excess nitrogen can pollute water and weaken plants. Under continuous cropping, maintain soil health by rotating crops, returning residues, adding manure or compost, controlling erosion, reducing unnecessary tillage and liming acid soils only when a test shows it is needed. Check local recommendations, because soils, crops and regulations differ by country.

keyPoints: Soil texture is the proportion of sand, silt and clay; structure is how particles form aggregates.
Good structure and organic matter improve root growth, water movement and nutrient storage.
Soil pH affects nutrient availability and root health; most crops prefer near-neutral pH but this varies.
CEC is the sum of exchangeable cations, measured in cmol(+)/kg; higher CEC reduces leaching.
Fertilisers may be inorganic or organic; apply them according to soil tests and crop needs.
Continuous cropping needs rotation, residues, manure or compost, erosion control and tested liming.

en.title: Crop Classification, Adaptation and Agro-Ecology
en.short: How crops are classified, how adaptation and agro-ecological zones work, and how climate sets limits.

sections.heading: Classifying crops
sections.text:
Crops are grouped by use, life cycle and botanical family. By use: cereals are grown for grain (maize, rice, sorghum); legumes for seed and nitrogen fixation (cowpea, groundnut, soybean); oil crops for oil (oil palm, sunflower); roots and tubers for swollen storage organs (cassava, yam, sweet potato); fibres for fibre (cotton, jute); beverages for drinks (tea, coffee, cocoa). These groups are practical, not botanical: groundnut is a legume and an oil crop.

By life cycle, an annual completes its life in one season (maize), a biennial takes two seasons and usually flowers in the second (onion, sugar beet), and a perennial lives for several years (cassava, oil palm). Botanical classification uses family, genus and species. Cereals belong to Poaceae, legumes to Fabaceae, and cassava to Euphorbiaceae. Family matters because relatives often share pests, diseases and growth habits.

sections.heading: Adaptation and zones
sections.text:
Adaptation is the set of traits that let a crop survive and reproduce in a given environment. A variety adapted to one zone may fail in another. An agro-ecological zone is an area with similar climate, soils and cropping patterns. In West Africa, common zones run from humid forest through derived and Guinea savanna to Sudan savanna and Sahel. Names and boundaries differ between countries and maps, so use local extension guides.

For example, cassava and plantain fit the humid forest, while sorghum and millet fit drier savanna. This is a case, not a fixed rule: irrigation, improved varieties and planting dates can shift limits.

sections.heading: Climate limits
sections.text: Temperature limits growth through cardinal temperatures: a minimum, an optimum and a maximum. Cool-season wheat and potato differ from warm-season maize. Day length, or photoperiod, controls flowering: short-day crops flower when nights are long, long-day crops when nights are short, and day-neutral crops are less sensitive. Rainfall limits crops through amount, seasonal distribution and evaporation. Rice suits flooded lowlands; sorghum and millet tolerate drier savanna. Match crop and variety to the zone, then use management to reduce risk.

keyPoints: Crops can be classified by use, life cycle and botanical family.
Cereals, legumes, oil crops, roots and tubers, fibres and beverages are use groups, not botanical groups.
Annuals complete their life in one season, biennials in two, and perennials live for several years.
Botanical family matters because related crops often share pests, diseases and growth habits.
Adaptation is the fit between a crop’s traits and its environment; an agro-ecological zone groups areas with similar climate, soils and cropping patterns.
Temperature, day length and rainfall set limits, but irrigation, variety choice and planting date can shift them.

en.title: Weather, Climate and the Cropping Calendar
en.short: Weather elements, planting dates, season length and how cropping calendars are built and used.

sections.heading: Weather and climate
sections.text:
Weather is the state of the atmosphere over hours or days: rainfall, temperature, sunlight, humidity and wind. Climate is the long-term pattern. Crops depend on both. Rainfall supplies soil water, temperature controls growth speed, solar radiation drives photosynthesis, and humidity and wind affect water loss. Evapotranspiration is water lost from soil and plants.

A crop responds to its own field, not a regional average. A short dry spell at flowering can cut yield even when seasonal rainfall is good, so calendars need local records.

sections.heading: Rainfall and temperature
sections.text:
Planting waits for enough rain to wet the seed zone and support establishment; the amount varies, so use local advice. Temperature has a base below which growth stops and an upper limit above which heat stress occurs. Season length is the period when water and temperature allow growth from planting to maturity. Late onset, early cessation or dry spells shorten it.

Growing degree days add heat above a base: GDD = (Tmax + Tmin) ÷ 2 − Tbase, with negative values set to zero.

sections.heading: Building a calendar
sections.text:
A cropping calendar lists operations and crop stages by week or month. Build it from long-term rainfall and temperature records, crop water and heat needs, soil water storage, and field-operation time. Use probabilities, not one average year: onset date, dry-spell risk and cessation date.

Illustrative example: a hypothetical crop needs 450 mm. Rain from May to August is 60, 140, 170 and 110 mm.
Cumulative rain: 60, 200, 370, 480 mm.
The target is passed in August, so planning should not treat the crop as water-secure before then.

sections.heading: Variability and planning
sections.text: Climate variability is year-to-year fluctuation around the average: early or late rains, hot days, dry spells. Climate change is a long-term shift in averages and extremes. Both affect planting dates, cultivar choice and harvest planning. Farmers can spread risk with several planting dates, suitable varieties and water storage, but use current local advice.

keyPoints: Weather is short-term atmospheric conditions; climate is the long-term pattern.
Rainfall amount and distribution set soil water and planting dates; temperature sets growth rate and limits.
Season length is the period when water and temperature allow growth from planting to maturity.
Growing degree days: GDD = (Tmax + Tmin) ÷ 2 − Tbase, with negative daily values set to zero.
A cropping calendar uses long-term local records, crop needs and probabilities, not one average year.
Climate variability is year-to-year fluctuation; climate change is a long-term shift, so use current local advice.

en.title: Land Preparation and Tillage Systems
en.short: Primary and secondary tillage, seedbeds, and comparing conventional, minimum and conservation systems.

sections.heading: Primary and secondary tillage
sections.text:
Tillage is the mechanical working of soil to prepare a seedbed. Primary tillage breaks and loosens soil deeply, using a mouldboard plough, disc plough, chisel plough or subsoiler. It leaves a rough surface; inversion ploughs also bury residue.

Secondary tillage follows with harrows, rotavators or rollers. It breaks clods, levels the surface, controls shallow weeds and firms the soil before sowing. Primary work is deeper and heavier; secondary work is shallower and finer.

sections.heading: Seedbed requirements
sections.text:
A good seedbed is firm, moist, weed-free and of even depth. Small seeds such as onion, carrot and lettuce need a fine, crumbly tilth and shallow sowing. Larger seeds such as maize and cowpea tolerate coarser soil.

Root and tuber crops such as carrot, potato and cassava need deep, loose soil for roots and tubers to swell. Rice is often grown in puddled soil (wet soil worked into a soft paste). In West Africa, yam and cassava are commonly planted on ridges.

sections.heading: Comparing tillage systems
sections.text:
Conventional tillage usually uses a mouldboard or disc plough plus harrow passes. It gives good weed control and a uniform seedbed but exposes soil, breaks aggregates and leaves little residue. Minimum tillage reduces passes, often with a chisel plough or strip till.

Conservation tillage limits disturbance and keeps residue cover, often at least 30% of the surface; definitions vary. No-till is the extreme. Conservation systems improve structure, cut erosion and conserve moisture, but soil may be cooler and wetter, and weeds or compaction may need management. Fewer passes cut fuel and labour costs, though herbicides may be needed.

sections.heading: Worked cost example
sections.text:
Suppose a plough costs 12,000 naira per hectare and each harrow pass 6,000. Conventional tillage with one ploughing and two harrowings costs 12,000 + (2 × 6,000) = 24,000 naira per hectare. Minimum tillage with one chisel pass at 10,000 and herbicide at 8,000 costs 18,000.

The saving is 6,000, or 25% of 24,000. Check: 6,000 ÷ 24,000 = 0.25. Prices vary, so use local figures. Cheaper is not always more profitable: yield, erosion and long-term soil health matter.

keyPoints: Primary tillage breaks soil deeply; secondary tillage refines and firms the seedbed.
Mouldboard and disc ploughs, chisel ploughs and subsoilers are primary implements; harrows, rotavators and rollers are secondary.
Small seeds need fine, shallow seedbeds; root crops need deep, loose soil; rice often needs puddled soil.
Conventional tillage gives a clean seedbed but exposes soil to erosion and organic matter loss.
Conservation tillage keeps residue cover, improves structure and conserves moisture, but may need more management.
Tillage cost = sum of passes × cost per pass, plus any herbicide; fewer passes usually cost less.

en.title: Planting Methods, Plant Population and Spacing
en.short: Sowing methods, seed rate, spacing, planting depth, plant population and how density affects yield.

sections.heading: Sowing and depth
sections.text: Sowing methods include broadcasting, drilling in rows, dibbling and transplanting. Broadcasting spreads seed by hand or machine; it is fast but gives uneven stands. Drilling places seed at a set row spacing and depth. Dibbling puts a few seeds in holes. Transplanting raises seedlings in a nursery first. Planting depth should follow the crop recommendation. Small seeds are sown shallow; large seeds can go deeper. Too deep uses up seed reserves; too shallow leaves seed in dry soil. Moisture, soil texture and temperature also affect emergence.

sections.heading: Population and spacing
sections.text: Plant population is the number of plants in a field, though in crop science it is usually expressed per unit area. This per-area figure is the plant population density, such as plants per hectare. For rectangular spacing, density = 1 ÷ (row spacing × plant spacing), with both distances in metres, giving plants per square metre. Multiply by 10,000 for plants per hectare. Example: rows 0.75 m apart and plants 0.25 m apart give 1 ÷ (0.75 × 0.25) = 5.33 plants/m², or 53,333 plants/ha. A 2 ha field then holds about 106,667 plants.

sections.heading: Seed rate and yield
sections.text: Seed rate is the mass of seed needed per area. Stand is the established plant population actually achieved. Seed rate must allow for germination and field establishment, so the target stand is divided by both fractions. Seed rate (kg/ha) = target plants/ha × 1000-seed weight (g) ÷ (1,000,000 × germination fraction × establishment fraction). Example: 100,000 plants/ha, 40 g per 1000 seeds, 90% germination and 80% establishment give 100,000 × 40 ÷ (1,000,000 × 0.9 × 0.8) = 5.56 kg/ha. Yield rises with density to an optimum, then levels off or falls. The optimum depends on cultivar, fertility, water and sowing date. Determinate cultivars, which stop stem growth once flowering begins, compensate less than tillering or branching ones; high fertility and water usually raise the optimum density.

keyPoints: Sowing methods include broadcasting, drilling, dibbling and transplanting.
Plant population density is plants per unit area; for rectangular spacing in metres, plants/m² = 1 ÷ (row spacing × plant spacing), and plants/ha = 10,000 ÷ (row spacing × plant spacing).
Seed rate (kg/ha) = target plants/ha × 1000-seed weight (g) ÷ (1,000,000 × germination fraction × establishment fraction).
Planting depth should follow crop recommendations: small seeds shallow, large seeds deeper, and never so deep that reserves are exhausted.
Yield rises with density to an optimum, then levels off or falls.
The optimum density depends on cultivar, fertility, water and sowing date.

en.title: Weeds and Their Management in Crops
en.short: Weed definitions, classification, crop loss assessment, control methods, herbicide modes of action and IWM.

sections.heading: What a weed is
sections.text: A weed is a plant growing where it is not wanted, especially where it competes with a crop for light, water and nutrients. Weeds are classified by life cycle, morphology and habitat. By life cycle: annual weeds complete their life in one season; biennials grow vegetatively in year one and flower in year two; perennials live for several years and often regrow from roots, rhizomes or tubers. By morphology: monocotyledons include grasses and sedges, while dicotyledons are broadleaved weeds. By habitat: terrestrial weeds grow on land, aquatic weeds grow in water or waterlogged soil, and parasitic weeds attach to crop roots or stems.

sections.heading: Crop loss and control
sections.text: Crop loss assessment compares a weed-free crop with a weedy crop, or relates loss to weed density. The common formula is: yield loss (%) = (weed-free yield − weedy yield) ÷ weed-free yield × 100. For example, if weed-free yield is 4.0 t/ha and weedy yield is 3.1 t/ha, loss = (4.0 − 3.1) ÷ 4.0 × 100 = 22.5%. Control methods work best together. Cultural control uses crop rotation, competitive cultivars, timely planting, adequate spacing, mulching and clean seed. Mechanical control uses hand weeding, hoeing, tillage and mowing. Biological control uses natural enemies that attack only the target weed, mainly against introduced weeds; it is slow and needs care.

sections.heading: Herbicides and IWM
sections.text: Chemical control uses herbicides. Herbicide groups are classified by mode of action, the biochemical process they block. Examples include photosynthesis inhibitors, ACCase (acetyl-CoA carboxylase) inhibitors that affect grass weeds, ALS (acetolactate synthase) inhibitors, synthetic auxins such as 2,4-D, and glyphosate, which inhibits EPSP synthase. Selectivity (ability to kill weeds without harming the crop), dose, timing and placement determine safety. Integrated weed management (IWM) combines monitoring, economic thresholds (weed levels where control pays), cultural, mechanical, biological and chemical methods. To avoid resistance, rotate herbicide modes of action, use labelled mixtures, include non-chemical controls, prevent weed seed set and clean equipment between fields.

keyPoints: A weed is a plant growing where it is not wanted.
Life cycle classes are annual, biennial and perennial.
Morphology classes include monocotyledons and dicotyledons; habitat classes include terrestrial and aquatic.
Yield loss (%) = (weed-free yield − weedy yield) ÷ weed-free yield × 100.
Integrated weed management combines cultural, mechanical, biological and chemical methods.
Rotate herbicide modes of action to slow resistance.

en.title: Insect and Mite Pests of Crops: Feeding Groups, Damage and Management
en.short: Feeding groups, crop damage, economic injury level, IPM, chemical and biological control, and safe pesticide handling.

sections.heading: Feeding groups and damage
sections.text: Insects and mites damage crops in two main ways. Chewing pests have mouthparts that bite and tear. Caterpillars, beetles and grasshoppers remove leaf tissue, bore into stems or fruits, and attack stored grain. Piercing-sucking pests have needle-like mouthparts. Aphids, whiteflies and mites suck sap, causing yellowing, stunting and leaf curl; thrips rasp the surface and suck, causing silvering. Many also transmit plant viruses. On cereals, stem borers and armyworms are chewing pests; aphids are sucking pests. On legumes, pod borers and bruchids (stored seeds) cause losses. Stored produce is attacked by weevils, grain borers and moths, causing weight loss and contamination. Mites are tiny arachnids, not insects, but cause similar stippling and webbing.

sections.heading: Economic injury level and IPM
sections.text: The economic injury level (EIL) is the pest density at which the cost of control equals the value of the yield loss it prevents. The economic threshold is slightly lower, prompting action before EIL is reached. For illustration, EIL = C ÷ (V × I), where C is control cost per hectare, V is crop value per tonne, and I is yield loss per pest per hectare. If C = 40 USD/ha, V = 250 USD/t, and I = 0.0002 t/ha per pest, then EIL = 40 ÷ (250 × 0.0002) = 800 pests/ha. Integrated pest management (IPM) combines monitoring, thresholds, cultural methods (resistant varieties, rotation, sanitation), physical methods, biological control and, only when needed, selective chemicals.

sections.heading: Control methods and safety
sections.text: Chemical control uses insecticides and acaricides. Rotate modes of action to slow resistance. Apply the correct dose at the right growth stage, and respect the pre-harvest interval. Safe handling means reading the label, wearing protective clothing, avoiding drift and disposing of containers properly. Biological control uses natural enemies: predators (ladybirds), parasitoids (wasps) and pathogens (Bt, fungi). Conservation and augmentation help. For example, in Nigeria maize farmers scout for fall armyworm, use resistant varieties and hand-pick egg masses; they spray only when thresholds are exceeded.

keyPoints: Chewing pests remove tissue or bore into plants and stored grain; piercing-sucking pests suck sap and often transmit viruses.
The economic injury level (EIL) is the pest density where control cost equals the value of prevented yield loss; the economic threshold is lower.
EIL = C ÷ (V × I), where C is control cost per hectare, V is crop value per tonne, and I is yield loss per pest per hectare.
Integrated pest management combines monitoring, thresholds, cultural, physical, biological and selective chemical methods.
Biological control uses predators, parasitoids and pathogens; conserve natural enemies.
Handle pesticides safely: read the label, wear protective clothing, respect pre-harvest intervals and dispose of containers properly.

en.title: Crop Diseases and Their Management
en.short: Fungal, bacterial, viral and nematode crop diseases, the disease triangle, cycles and integrated control.

sections.heading: Pathogen groups
sections.text: A pathogen is any organism that causes disease. Fungi are eukaryotic, usually filamentous, and spread by spores; they cause leaf spots, blights, rots and wilts. Bacteria are single-celled prokaryotes that enter through wounds or natural openings and multiply in plant tissue; they cause spots, soft rots and wilts, and may ooze from lesions. Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites with no cell wall; they spread by vectors such as aphids and whiteflies, by cuttings or sometimes seed, and cause mosaic, mottling, yellowing and stunting. Plant-parasitic nematodes are microscopic roundworms with a stylet; they damage roots and some transmit viruses.

sections.heading: Disease triangle and cycle
sections.text: Disease develops under the disease triangle: a susceptible host, a virulent pathogen and a favourable environment must coincide. Time is often added as a fourth factor. A disease cycle describes how a pathogen survives, produces inoculum, disperses, infects, colonises, produces symptoms and reproduces. Some pathogens complete one cycle per season; others have many cycles, so they spread faster.

sections.heading: Symptoms and diagnosis
sections.text: Symptoms include leaf spots, blights, wilts, rots, cankers, galls, mosaics and stunting. Signs are the pathogen itself, such as fungal growth, bacterial ooze or nematode cysts. Diagnosis uses field signs, host identity and laboratory tests; a plant clinic or extension service can help.

sections.heading: Control tools
sections.text:
Integrated management combines resistant varieties, cultural practices, biological agents and fungicides. Resistant varieties are often the cheapest control, but resistance can break down when pathogen races change. Cultural practices include clean seed and cuttings, rotation, sanitation, roguing (removing infected plants), spacing and water management. Biological agents such as Trichoderma and Bacillus can suppress pathogens, though results vary. Fungicides protect or cure fungal diseases; they do not control viruses, and bacterial control is limited. Follow labels and rotate modes of action to slow resistance.

Case: Amaka grows cassava in Oyo State, Nigeria. Plants show mosaic, leaf distortion and stunting, symptoms of cassava mosaic disease spread by whitefly and infected cuttings. She uses certified clean cuttings and resistant varieties, removes infected plants and avoids moving cuttings.

keyPoints: The disease triangle requires a susceptible host, a virulent pathogen and a favourable environment.
Fungi, bacteria, viruses and nematodes differ in structure, spread and the symptoms they cause.
A disease cycle runs from inoculum and dispersal through infection, colonisation, symptoms and survival.
Symptoms are what the plant shows; signs are the pathogen or its structures.
Integrated management combines resistant varieties, cultural practices, biological agents and fungicides.
Fungicides control fungal diseases, not viruses, and resistance management is essential.

en.title: Crop Nutrition and Fertiliser Use
en.short: Deficiency and toxicity diagnosis, fertiliser types, placement, timing, efficiency and simple recommendations.

sections.heading: Symptoms and diagnosis
sections.text:
Deficiency symptoms reflect nutrient mobility. Nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and magnesium are mobile, so deficiency appears first on older leaves: pale green or yellowing for nitrogen, dark green or purplish leaves for phosphorus, marginal scorch for potassium, and yellowing between veins for magnesium. Calcium, iron, boron and sulphur are less mobile, so symptoms appear on young growth: distorted tips, yellowing between veins or poor growing points. Toxicity, such as boron or manganese excess, may cause dead edges or stunting. Symptoms are clues, not proof, because drought, waterlogging, pests, diseases and herbicide injury can mimic them.

Soil tests measure pH, organic matter and available nutrients; plant tissue tests compare leaf concentrations with critical ranges for the crop and stage. Use both, with local calibration, before deciding.

sections.heading: Fertiliser types and use
sections.text: Fertilisers are straight (one main nutrient, such as urea, 46% N) or compound and blended (two or more, such as NPK). They may be granular, liquid or foliar; organic manures add nutrients slowly. Placement puts fertiliser where roots can reach it. Broadcast suits dense crops and lime; banding or dibbling near the seed reduces fixation and weed uptake, but fertiliser must not touch the seed. Nitrogen is usually split: a basal dose and one or two top dressings. Nutrient use efficiency (NUE) is crop output per unit nutrient applied. The 4R idea, right source, rate, time and place, raises NUE and cuts losses.

sections.heading: Simple recommendation
sections.text:
Suppose a soil test and local calibration recommend 60 kg N, 30 kg P2O5 and 30 kg K2O per hectare. Using urea (46% N), single superphosphate (18% P2O5) and muriate of potash (60% K2O):
Urea = 60 ÷ 0.46 = 130 kg/ha.
Single superphosphate = 30 ÷ 0.18 = 167 kg/ha.
Muriate of potash = 30 ÷ 0.60 = 50 kg/ha.
Apply P and K as a band before planting; split N, half basal and half at the recommended growth stage. Check current local recommendations.

keyPoints: Mobile nutrients such as nitrogen, potassium and magnesium show deficiency first on older leaves; less mobile nutrients such as calcium and iron show it on young growth.
Symptoms are not proof: confirm with soil tests, plant tissue tests and local calibration.
Straight fertilisers supply one main nutrient; compound or blended fertilisers supply several, and placement and timing affect losses.
Split nitrogen application and band phosphorus and potassium near roots, but keep fertiliser off the seed.
Nutrient use efficiency is crop output per unit nutrient applied; agronomic efficiency = (yield with fertiliser − yield without fertiliser) ÷ nutrient applied.
Fertiliser product needed = recommended nutrient ÷ fraction of nutrient in the product; for example 60 kg N ÷ 0.46 = 130 kg urea/ha.

en.title: Crop Water Management and Irrigation
en.short: Crop water needs, evapotranspiration, irrigation scheduling, system choice, efficiency, drainage, salinity.

sections.heading: Crop water use
sections.text:
Crop water requirement is the depth of water a crop needs over a season, mainly to replace evapotranspiration (ET). ET is evaporation from soil plus transpiration through leaves. Reference evapotranspiration (ETo) estimates demand for a standard crop under local weather. A crop coefficient (Kc) adjusts it: ETc = Kc × ETo. In mm, 1 mm over 1 hectare is 10 m³ of water.

Worked example: ETo = 5 mm/day and Kc = 0.8 give ETc = 4 mm/day. Over 10 days the crop uses 40 mm. With 12 mm effective rain, net irrigation need is 28 mm. At 70% application efficiency, the fraction of applied water stored in the root zone, gross irrigation = 28 ÷ 0.70 = 40 mm.

sections.heading: Scheduling irrigation
sections.text: Irrigation scheduling decides when and how much to apply. Indicators include soil moisture measured by tension or content, a water balance of rainfall, ET and irrigation, pan evaporation, and crop signs such as leaf rolling. Allowable depletion is how much plant-available water may be used before stress. Apply only enough to refill the root zone; overwatering wastes water and leaches nutrients.

sections.heading: System comparison
sections.text: Surface systems, such as basin and furrow, let water flow over the field by gravity. They are cheap but need level land and can be uneven. Sprinklers spray water like rain; they suit uneven land but lose water to wind and evaporation and need energy. Drip systems release water slowly through emitters near roots. They give high water use efficiency, the yield or biomass produced per unit water, but cost more and need filtration against clogging.

sections.heading: Drainage and salinity
sections.text: Drainage removes excess water through surface channels or subsurface pipes. Poor irrigation, especially overwatering without drainage, fills soil pores and causes waterlogging, where roots lack oxygen. In dry climates, salts in irrigation water remain as water evaporates. Repeated poor irrigation raises salinity, reducing water uptake. Prevention needs correct scheduling, efficient application, drainage and controlled leaching.

keyPoints: Crop water requirement is mainly the water needed to replace evapotranspiration.
ETc = Kc × ETo, where ETo is reference evapotranspiration and Kc is the crop coefficient.
Gross irrigation = net irrigation ÷ application efficiency.
Schedule irrigation using soil moisture, water balance, evaporation or crop stress, and refill only the root zone.
Surface, sprinkler and drip systems differ in cost, uniformity and water use efficiency.
Overirrigation without drainage causes waterlogging; in dry areas it also causes salinity.

en.title: Cropping Systems, Rotation and Intercropping
en.short: Sole, mixed, intercropping, relay and sequential systems, rotation, legumes and land equivalent ratio.

sections.heading: System types
sections.text: Sole cropping is one crop grown alone in a field in a season. Mixed cropping grows two or more crops together, often broadcast without distinct rows. Intercropping also grows crops together, but in a planned arrangement such as alternate rows. Relay cropping plants the second crop in the standing first crop before harvest, so they overlap. Sequential cropping grows crops one after another with no overlap; double cropping is two sequential crops in one year.

sections.heading: Land equivalent ratio
sections.text: The land equivalent ratio (LER) compares sole-crop land with intercrop land. For each crop, divide intercrop yield by sole-crop yield, then add the ratios: LER = Σ(Yi intercropped ÷ Yi sole), where Yi is yield of crop i. LER above 1 means intercropping is more efficient; below 1 means less efficient. Example: sole maize yields 4 t/ha and sole cowpea 2 t/ha. Intercropped, maize yields 2.8 t/ha and cowpea 1.2 t/ha. LER = 2.8 ÷ 4 + 1.2 ÷ 2 = 0.7 + 0.6 = 1.3, so 1 ha intercrop equals 1.3 ha sole crops.

sections.heading: Rotation and legumes
sections.text: Rotation is growing different crops in a planned order on the same land. It helps break pest and disease cycles, improves weed control, spreads labour, and can improve soil structure and nutrient balance. Legumes such as cowpea and soybean form nodules with rhizobia and fix atmospheric nitrogen. Their residues can benefit a following cereal, but the amount fixed and left varies with the legume, soil, inoculant and management. In intercrops, legumes may add nitrogen but compete for light, water and nutrients.

sections.heading: Choosing a system
sections.text: Choice depends on the farm and agro-ecological zone, an area with similar climate and soils. Consider rainfall and season length, soil, slope, labour, capital, market, food needs and risk. A short-rainfall savanna may suit a cereal-legume intercrop for risk spreading and soil cover. A humid area with a long season may allow sequential or relay cropping. Test options on a small area and check local extension advice.

keyPoints: Sole cropping grows one crop alone; mixed and intercropping grow two or more together, with intercropping using a planned row or strip arrangement.
Relay cropping overlaps two crops, while sequential cropping grows them one after another with no overlap.
LER = Σ(Yi intercropped ÷ Yi sole); above 1 means intercropping uses land more efficiently, below 1 less efficiently.
Rotation helps break pest and disease cycles, improve weed control and balance nutrients.
Legumes fix atmospheric nitrogen with rhizobia, but the benefit to the next crop varies with the legume, soil and management.
System choice depends on rainfall, season length, soil, labour, market, food needs and risk in the local agro-ecological zone.

en.title: Crop Growth Analysis and Yield Components
en.short: Yield components for cereals, legumes and roots, growth analysis measures and a worked yield estimate.

sections.heading: Yield components
sections.text: Yield components are the parts that multiply to give yield. In cereals, grain yield = fertile ears or panicles per unit area × grains per ear or panicle × mean grain weight. Ears per area = plants per area × fertile ears per plant. In grain legumes, seed yield = plants per unit area × pods per plant × seeds per pod × mean seed weight. In root and tuber crops, yield = plants per unit area × storage roots or tubers per plant × mean root or tuber weight. A low stand may be partly offset by more tillers, pods or tubers per plant. This is compensatory growth. Compensation is limited, so plant population and uniformity matter.

sections.heading: Growth analysis
sections.text: Growth analysis follows dry matter and leaf area over time. Leaf area index (LAI) is leaf area divided by ground area. Crop growth rate (CGR) is dry matter gained per ground area per day: CGR = (W2 − W1) ÷ (t2 − t1), in g m−2 day−1. Relative growth rate (RGR) is gain per existing mass: RGR = (ln W2 − ln W1) ÷ (t2 − t1), in g g−1 day−1. Net assimilation rate (NAR) is CGR ÷ LAI. Leaf area duration (LAD) is mean LAI × days. Early LAI and LAD build grains per ear or pods per plant; grain filling sets grain weight.

sections.heading: Worked field estimate
sections.text: Take a wheat field sampled in several 1 m² quadrats. Mean stand is 220 plants per m², with 2.5 fertile ears per plant, 32 grains per ear and a 1000-grain weight of 40 g. Ears per m²: 220 × 2.5 = 550. Grains per m²: 550 × 32 = 17,600. Grain weight: 17,600 × (40 ÷ 1000) = 704 g per m². Convert: 704 × 10,000 = 7,040,000 g per ha = 7,040 kg per ha = 7.04 t per ha. Use a stated moisture basis and random quadrats; the sample must represent the field.

keyPoints: Cereal grain yield = fertile ears or panicles per unit area × grains per ear or panicle × mean grain weight.
Grain legume seed yield = plants per unit area × pods per plant × seeds per pod × mean seed weight.
Root and tuber yield = plants per unit area × storage roots or tubers per plant × mean root or tuber weight.
Compensatory growth lets a low stand be partly offset by more ears, pods or tubers per plant, but compensation is limited.
CGR = (W2 − W1) ÷ (t2 − t1); RGR = (ln W2 − ln W1) ÷ (t2 − t1); LAI = leaf area ÷ ground area.
Check a yield component estimate against a measured sample, a stated moisture basis and random quadrats.

en.title: Harvesting, Threshing and Postharvest Handling
en.short: Maturity indices, harvesting, threshing, drying, storage pests and simple loss assessment.

sections.heading: Maturity and harvesting
sections.text: Maturity indices are signs that a crop is ready to harvest. Physiological maturity is when seed dry matter is complete; harvest maturity is when the crop is ready to harvest with good quality and little loss. For grains, indices include days after planting, colour change, hard grain and moisture content. For legumes, pod colour and seed firmness matter; harvest before pods shatter. For tubers, vine senescence and skin set, where the skin does not rub off, are useful signs. Harvest grains with a sickle or combine; legumes by hand pulling or mower; tubers with a hoe, fork or lifter, avoiding cuts. Delayed harvest raises shattering, lodging and rot.

sections.heading: Threshing and drying
sections.text: Threshing separates grain or seed from heads or pods. Methods include beating, trampling and mechanical threshers; adjust speed to avoid cracking. Drying lowers moisture so moulds and insects cannot grow. Moisture content is usually given on a wet basis: MC% = (wet weight − dry weight) ÷ wet weight × 100. Example: 100 kg grain contains 85 kg dry matter and 15 kg water, so MC = 15 ÷ 100 × 100 = 15%. Drying to 13% gives total weight 85 ÷ 0.87 = 97.7 kg. Safe moisture varies by crop and climate; check local extension advice.

sections.heading: Storage and pests
sections.text: Store dry, clean grain in cribs, granaries, silos or hermetic (airtight) bags; tubers need cool, ventilated, dark stores. Main pests are insects such as weevils, grain borers and bruchids (legume seed weevils), plus rodents and moulds. Mould can produce aflatoxin. Losses rise with poor drying, dirty stores and long storage.

sections.heading: Assessing losses
sections.text: Simple loss assessment samples a known weight before and after storage. Percentage weight loss = (initial weight − final weight) ÷ initial weight × 100, but this includes water loss, so adjust for moisture. A count method is: percentage damaged grains = damaged grains ÷ total grains sampled × 100. Repeat samples at intervals during storage to estimate loss.

keyPoints: Maturity indices show when a crop has reached harvest quality.
Harvest legumes before pods shatter and tubers after skin set.
Thresh carefully to avoid cracking or bruising grain and seed.
Moisture content, wet basis = (wet weight − dry weight) ÷ wet weight × 100.
Percentage storage weight loss = (initial weight − final weight) ÷ initial weight × 100, corrected for moisture.
Percentage damaged grains = damaged grains ÷ total grains sampled × 100.

en.title: Seed Production, Quality and Certification
en.short: Seed classes, multiplication, isolation, roguing, purity and germination testing, treatment and certification.

sections.heading: Seed classes
sections.text: Seed classes show how close a lot is to the breeder’s stock. Breeder seed is produced by the plant breeder from maintained parent material; it has the highest genetic purity. Foundation seed is grown from breeder seed under careful management. Certified seed is grown from foundation seed, inspected and tested, and sold for crop production. Commercial seed is the certified seed farmers buy, though in some countries the term means truthfully labelled seed, which is sold on the producer’s own label rather than certified. Some systems add a registered class. Names and rules vary by country.

sections.heading: Multiplication and isolation
sections.text: A multiplication programme moves from small pure lots to large uniform lots: breeder to foundation to certified. Each stage needs clean land, approved parent seed, isolation, roguing, field inspection, careful harvest and records. Isolation stops pollen or seed from other varieties, crops or weeds entering the lot. It can be spatial (distance), temporal (different planting dates) or physical (barriers); the required distance depends on crop and national standard. Roguing removes off-type, diseased and weed plants before flowering and again before harvest. For example, planting 20 kg and harvesting 1,500 kg gives a multiplication ratio of 1,500 ÷ 20 = 75:1, an illustration only.

sections.heading: Testing, treatment and certification
sections.text: Seed testing uses a representative sample. The purity test separates pure seed, other crop seed, weed seed and inert matter, and reports percentages. The germination test counts normal seedlings under standard conditions, also as a percentage. Seed treatment applies fungicide or insecticide to protect seed and seedlings, or rhizobium inoculant to legume seed to improve nodulation and nitrogen fixation; treated seed must be labelled and never eaten. National seed certification services set standards, license producers, inspect fields, test samples, and issue certificates and labels. Examples are the National Agricultural Seeds Council in Nigeria and KEPHIS (Kenya Plant Health Inspectorate Service) in Kenya. Rules differ by country; check the current national seed law.

keyPoints: Breeder seed comes from the breeder and is the purest source; foundation and certified seed are multiplied from it in turn.
Commercial seed is usually certified seed sold to farmers, but the term varies by country.
Isolation and roguing prevent genetic contamination and off-types in the seed field.
Purity testing measures clean seed versus weed seed, other crop seed and inert matter; germination testing measures normal seedlings.
Seed treatment protects seed and seedlings, and treated seed must be clearly labelled.
National certification services inspect fields, test samples and certify seed; their rules are country-specific.

en.title: Plant Breeding Methods for Crop Improvement
en.short: Objectives, mating systems, selection, hybridisation, hybrid seed, G×E testing, mutation and polyploidy.

sections.heading: Objectives and mating systems
sections.text: Breeding starts with clear objectives: higher yield, better quality, earlier maturity, and resistance to pests, diseases, drought or lodging. A trait must be heritable and measurable. The mating system, how a crop naturally pollinates and reproduces, guides the method. Self-pollinated crops, such as rice and wheat, naturally inbreed, so pure lines are useful. Cross-pollinated crops, such as maize and many grasses, outcross, so populations stay variable and mass selection or hybrid breeding fits. Mixed mating crops need care with isolation.

sections.heading: Selection methods
sections.text: Mass selection means choosing many good plants and bulking their seed. It is simple and cheap, but the parentage is unknown, so gain is slow. Pure line selection means selecting one superior self-pollinated plant and testing its selfed progeny. Because the line is homozygous, it breeds true. Selection response can be predicted as R = h² × S, where h² is heritability and S is the selection differential. If h² = 0.4 and selected plants average 0.5 t/ha above the population mean, expected gain is 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2 t/ha.

sections.heading: Hybridisation and hybrid seed
sections.text: Hybridisation crosses genetically different parents to combine traits. A single cross is the F1 of two inbred lines. Backcrossing moves one trait, such as disease resistance, into a good variety. Hybrid seed production needs isolation to stop unwanted pollen. In maize, breeders detassel the female rows, or use cytoplasmic male sterility, so seed is set only by the chosen male. Farmers must buy fresh F1 seed each season because the next generation segregates.

sections.heading: Testing, release and new variation
sections.text: Genotype by environment interaction, G × E, means varieties rank differently across sites or seasons. Breeders therefore test advanced lines in replicated trials over several locations and years. Release rules differ by country; check the national variety release committee. Mutation breeding uses physical or chemical mutagens to create new variation, useful when desired traits are scarce. Polyploidy breeding doubles chromosome sets, often with colchicine. It can change size, fertility and stress tolerance, but results vary.

keyPoints: Breeding objectives must match heritable traits and farmer or market needs.
Mating system decides the method: pure lines suit self-pollinated crops, mass selection and hybrids suit cross-pollinated crops.
Mass selection bulks many selected plants; pure line selection tests the selfed progeny of one plant.
Response to selection is R = h² × S.
Hybrid seed is F1 seed from chosen inbred parents and must be produced under isolation each season.
G × E requires multi-location and multi-year testing before release; mutation and polyploidy can widen variation.

en.title: Crop Biotechnology and Genetically Modified Crops
en.short: Covers tissue culture, marker-assisted selection, GM crops, traits, benefits, risks, regulation and labelling.

sections.heading: Tissue culture
sections.text: Tissue culture means growing small pieces of plant tissue on a sterile nutrient medium, with sugar, minerals and hormones, to form shoots and roots. It is also called micropropagation when used to make many identical plants. It is not genetic modification. It is used for disease-free planting material and rapid clonal multiplication in banana, plantain, cassava, potato, sugarcane and oil palm. It also helps breeders rescue embryos and produce doubled haploids.

sections.heading: Marker-assisted selection
sections.text: Marker-assisted selection uses a DNA test for a marker, a short DNA sequence linked to a useful gene, to choose plants in a breeding programme. The breeder can test seedlings instead of waiting for the plant to show the trait. It is most reliable for traits controlled by one or a few genes, such as disease resistance. Rice with the Sub1 gene for submergence tolerance was bred this way. It is not genetic modification; it only guides conventional crossing.

sections.heading: Genetic modification
sections.text: Genetic modification, or genetic engineering, changes a plant’s DNA directly, often by moving a gene from another species. The plant is then called transgenic. Common traits are insect resistance from Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) genes in maize and cotton, herbicide tolerance in soybean, maize and cotton, and virus resistance in papaya. Golden Rice was developed to make provitamin A (beta-carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A) in the grain. Gene editing is a newer method that can change the plant’s own DNA without adding a foreign gene; its regulation varies.

sections.heading: Benefits and debate
sections.text: Supporters say GM crops can cut pest losses, reduce spraying and raise food quality. Critics warn of gene flow (transgenes escaping into wild relatives or other crops), resistant pests, effects on non-target species, allergenicity and seed costs. Evidence is case-specific. Many countries regulate GM crops through biosafety laws, approving each crop and trait separately. Labelling rules differ: some countries require it, others use disclosure or voluntary systems. Rules change, so check the current regulator, such as Nigeria’s NBMA (National Biosafety Management Agency) or the European Commission.

keyPoints: Tissue culture grows plant tissue on sterile medium to make clones or clean planting material; it is not GM.
Marker-assisted selection uses DNA markers linked to genes to speed conventional breeding, especially for simple traits.
Genetic modification inserts or alters DNA directly, often across species, to give traits such as Bt insect resistance or herbicide tolerance.
Benefits and risks of GM crops are case-specific and should be assessed crop by crop and trait by trait.
Biosafety regulation and labelling rules differ by country and change, so check the current official source.
Gene editing is distinct from older transgenic methods and its regulation varies.

en.title: Climate Change, Crop Adaptation and Resilience
en.short: How heat, rainfall shifts and CO2 affect crops, and how farmers adapt and store soil carbon.

sections.heading: Climate stresses
sections.text: Rising temperature speeds crop development, so grain filling may be shorter and yield lower. Heat stress at flowering can reduce pollination, especially in cereals. Shifting rainfall makes planting dates less reliable and raises drought or flood risk. Higher carbon dioxide (CO2) often increases photosynthesis in C3 crops such as wheat and rice more than in C4 crops such as maize and sorghum. But gains vary, and grain protein or micronutrients may fall. Pests and diseases may extend their range or produce more generations in warmer seasons. Water supply changes because warmer air raises evaporation and plants may use water differently.

sections.heading: Adaptation options
sections.text: Adaptation means adjusting farming so crops cope with the new conditions; resilience is the ability to recover after shocks. Stress-tolerant varieties bred for heat, drought or salinity help, but they must suit local markets and soils. Adjusted planting dates and shorter-season varieties can match rainfall and avoid heat at flowering. Soil moisture conservation includes mulching, tied ridges, contour farming and organic matter to improve infiltration. Diversification spreads risk, and irrigation reduces reliance on rainfall.

sections.heading: Soil carbon mitigation
sections.text: Mitigation means reducing greenhouse gases or storing carbon. Soil organic carbon is carbon held in soil organic matter. Adding crop residues, manure, compost and reducing tillage can build soil carbon, which also improves water holding. But storage is limited and reversible; it is not a substitute for cutting emissions. Measure changes with soil tests over years.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Suppose a crop needs 550 mm of water in a season. If rainfall falls from 600 mm to 480 mm, the fall is (600 − 480) ÷ 600 × 100 = 20%. The crop then faces a deficit of 550 − 480 = 70 mm, which must come from stored soil water or irrigation. Mulch and early planting can reduce that gap, but they do not create water.

keyPoints: Warmer temperatures can shorten grain filling and damage flowering.
Elevated CO2 often benefits C3 crops more than C4 crops, but quality may fall.
Adaptation includes stress-tolerant varieties, adjusted planting dates and soil moisture conservation.
Resilience is the capacity to recover after climate shocks.
Soil carbon can be built with residues, manure and reduced tillage, but storage is limited.
Water deficit = crop water requirement − available water; a fall from 600 mm to 480 mm is 20%.

en.title: Pasture and Forage Crops
en.short: Main pasture grasses and legumes, establishment, grazing, carrying capacity, hay, silage and feed value.

sections.heading: Forage species
sections.text: Pasture is land grazed by livestock; forage is plant material cut or grazed as feed. Grasses supply energy and fibre. Tropical examples include guinea grass (Megathyrsus maximus), elephant grass (Pennisetum purpureum) and Rhodes grass (Chloris gayana); temperate examples include perennial ryegrass (Lolium perenne). Legumes supply protein and fix nitrogen with rhizobia. Examples are white clover (Trifolium repens), lucerne (Medicago sativa) and stylo (Stylosanthes spp.). Grass-legume mixtures balance fibre and protein.

sections.heading: Establishment and grazing
sections.text: Prepare a weed-free seedbed, use tested seed, sow at the locally recommended depth and rate, and control weeds early. Inoculate legume seed with the correct rhizobium where needed. Supply phosphorus and potassium; nodulated legumes usually need little nitrogen. Avoid grazing too soon, so roots and crowns establish. Manage by stocking rate, rest periods, cutting height, fertiliser and weed control. Systems include continuous grazing, rotational grazing with rested paddocks, strip grazing, deferred grazing and zero grazing or cut-and-carry. Rotational grazing can improve persistence and use, but needs fencing, water and planning.

sections.heading: Carrying capacity
sections.text:
Carrying capacity is the number of animals a pasture can support over a stated period without decline. It depends on usable dry matter (DM), animal intake and season.
Carrying capacity (animals/ha) = DM yield × utilisation ÷ (daily intake × days).
Example: yield 8,000 kg DM/ha/year, utilisation 0.60, animal 250 kg eating 2.5% of body weight daily.
Usable DM = 8,000 × 0.60 = 4,800 kg.
Daily intake = 250 × 0.025 = 6.25 kg DM.
Annual intake = 6.25 × 365 = 2,281 kg DM.
Carrying capacity = 4,800 ÷ 2,281 = 2.1 animals/ha.

sections.heading: Hay and silage
sections.text: Make hay by cutting and drying forage to safe moisture, then baling and storing dry. Make silage by wilting, chopping, compacting and sealing forage; lactic acid bacteria ferment sugars and lower pH. Both conserve feed but lose dry matter. Feeding value depends on digestibility, crude protein, fibre and minerals. Young forage is better than stemmy forage; legumes are higher in protein, grasses in fibre.

keyPoints: Grasses provide energy and fibre; legumes provide protein and fix nitrogen with rhizobia.
Establish pasture with tested seed, correct legume inoculation, weed control and rest before grazing.
Carrying capacity = DM yield × utilisation ÷ (daily intake × days).
Rotational grazing rests paddocks and can improve persistence, but needs fencing, water and planning.
Hay is dried forage; silage is fermented, sealed forage that preserves moist feed.
Forage quality falls with maturity; test feed and balance rations.

en.title: Industrial and Plantation Crops
en.short: Production, harvest and first processing of tropical cotton, oil palm, cocoa, sugarcane and rubber.

sections.heading: Crops and uses
sections.text: Industrial crops supply raw materials for processing and trade. Plantation crops are usually perennials grown on estates or by smallholders and processed soon after harvest. The tropical groups are fibre (cotton), oil (oil palm), beverage (cocoa), sugar (sugarcane) and latex (rubber). Uses include cotton lint for textiles, palm oil for food and soap, cocoa for chocolate and drinks, sugar and jaggery from cane, and rubber for tyres and latex goods. Cotton is annual; oil palm, cocoa and rubber are perennial; sugarcane is a grass grown as a plant or ratoon (regrowth) crop.

sections.heading: Establishment and harvest
